extracted.intended_audience: physicians and educated general readers interested in neurology/psychopathology (late-19th-century clinical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Clinical and phenomenological criteria for recognizing, characterizing, and treating hysteria (hystero-epilepsy) and for distinguishing it from claimed demoniacal possession; includes diagnostic signs, course of attacks, and therapeutic observations (metallotherapy/magnetotherapy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of sensibility (tactual, muscular, pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The skin and muscles have distinct modes of sensibility: tactual sensibility perceives contact; there is also perception of temperature/consistency; muscular sensibility gives awareness of movement and execution; sensibility to pain is a separate mode provoked by injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions when assessing sensory deficits — determine whether a deficit affects tactual contact, temperature/consistency perception, muscular sense (position/movement), or pain sensation. Examples: pin-prick tests for cutaneous tactual sensibility; observe awareness of voluntary movement for muscular sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical definition of anaesthesia in hysteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysteric anaesthesia: absence of sensibility such that patients do not perceive pin-pricks, burns, or cuts; they may be pricked/scratched without any intimation of being wounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate anaesthesia clinically by light pin-prick tests (with eyes bandaged to exclude visual cues). Note that anaesthesia may be general or regionally limited; persistent lack of sensation to typical stimuli supports diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial / localized anaesthesia and small insensible zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial anaesthesia can occur even in slightly hysterical patients; small localized zones of insensibility may be found on careful testing (pricking skin lightly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map sensory thresholds across regions systematically — a small discrete insensible patch is compatible with hysteria. Beware of assuming uniform deficits; look for sharply demarcated islands of insensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemianesthesia with sharp midline boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysteric hemianesthesia is often limited to one side of the body and so exactly limited that moving two or three millimetres across the median line establishes presence or absence of sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lateral boundaries precisely; a sensory boundary very close to the midline (within millimetres) is characteristic of functional/ hysteric distribution rather than organic nerve lesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of structural/organic lesion
rubrics_metrics.description: No material organic injury is connected with hysteria: affected nerves, marrow, and brain show no swelling or haemorrhage; long-standing hemisensory deficits may disappear abruptly without trace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret negative structural findings (no observable nerve/brain lesion) and reversibility as evidence against organic pathology and in favor of a dynamic (functional) nervous perversion. Use longitudinal observation to confirm abrupt, unexplained recovery as supportive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capriciousness and sudden reversibility of symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysterical maladies are uncertain, changing, capricious — they can come on without known cause and disappear suddenly (sometimes after trivial emotion); prolonged paralysis may be suddenly reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the lability of symptoms (onset/offset variability) when differentiating hysteria from structural disease. A trivial emotional event precipitating recovery argues for functional etiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolonged abstinence and apparent preservation of health
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hysterical patients may remain a very long time without taking food or drink, with secretions apparently suspended, and yet preserve plumpness and usual appearance of health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret prolonged fasting as supernatural; investigate for possible simulation or unusual physiological adaptation. Be cautious about claims of miraculous fasting and verify via observation when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of intentional simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patients habitually attempt simulations (e.g., feigning lack of eating) for motives that may not be evidently self-benefiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful surveillance and corroborative observation (as in historical example of Barbara) to exclude deliberate deception. Maintain clinical skepticism and verify extraordinary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metallotherapy: metal application restores sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of pieces of metals (gold, silver, copper, zinc) to the insensible region can produce complete restoration of sensibility in a few hours; different patients respond to different metals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider topical metal application as a therapeutic/diagnostic maneuver in anaesthetic hysteria. Expect variable efficacy; record which metal produces change. The proposed mechanism is development of feeble electric currents from metal–moist skin contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetotherapy: magnet transfers anaesthesia
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnets, akin to very feeble electric currents, act like metals but instead of curing anaesthesia, they transfer it from one side to the other — e.g., applying a magnet to the insensitive right side may restore right-side sensibility while left side loses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magnet application as a demonstration of functional mobility of the morbid spot; the facility with which anaesthesia is moved argues against deep material lesions of nervous centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-period structure of the hystero-epileptic (demoniac) fit
rubrics_metrics.description: The demoniac/hystero-epileptic attack embraces three well-characterized periods: (1) first period analogous to epilepsy — abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening, convulsive trembling, followed by deep sleep; (2) second period of 'clownism' — prodigious bounds, contortions, self-injurious acts, violent behavior; (3) third period with return of cerebral life and vivid, often thematic hallucinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing an attack, classify signs by period. Use the presence of this structured sequence (rather than random convulsions) to support diagnosis of hystero-epilepsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate stoppability of second-period behavior by abdominal compression (ovarian pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent second-period fits can be stopped at once by compressing the abdomen at the point corresponding to the ovary; compression maintains consciousness and suppresses the rage until released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply controlled abdominal compression at the ovarian region as an emergency or diagnostic maneuver; reproducible cessation of the attack with ovary pressure suggests a hysteric/ovarian-related origin of the attack. Note patients may maintain orderliness while compression is sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and stereotypy of attacks and hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite violent appearance, the attacks are regular and punctual: symptoms appear in a predictable sequence; each patient tends to have a peculiar, repeating form of delirium (same personages/scenes) and the order of hallucinations does not vary between attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document consistency across attacks — repeated, stereotyped hallucinations and predictable terminal signs (e.g., military music, railroad noise, appearance of certain animals) support hysteria and allow prognosis of attack phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of hallucinations tied to antecedent life events
rubrics_metrics.description: The hallucinations in hysteria usually resemble real episodes of the patient's life, particularly the event that played the biggest role in the development of the malady; an exterior provocation (fright, grief, disillusion) often determines the first crisis and later shapes hallucination content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the patient's history for a precipitating event; a strong association between hallucination themes and personal past events differentiates hysterical delirium from other forms of insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from insanity/delirium of other causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysteric delirium differs from the delirium of the insane in that hysteric visions are nearly always determined by antecedent incidents, whereas the visions of the insane generally have no immediate relation to prior events; beast/monster visions can occur in many delirious states (fever, alcohol) but etiologies differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use etiology and thematic relation to prior events to distinguish hysteria from primary psychosis or toxic delirium. Consider other causes (fever, alcohol) when assessing similar visual phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclassification of historical 'demoniacal' phenomena as disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena historically attributed to demoniacal possession (convulsions, contortions, rollings) are in fact classifiable disease states (hystero-epilepsy) with identifiable phases and reproducible signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret historical accounts of 'possession' in light of contemporary clinical classification; apply present-day observation and categorization rather than supernatural explanations.
